messages.subject: Re: pouplation distribution parameter estimation
messages.subject_clean: pouplation distribution parameter estimation
messages.body_plain:
Thanks. Using the posterior theta distribution to update population parameters is consistent with setting the first derivatives of population parameters to 0.  However, it does not work if the number of quadrature points is small (say <20 for two dimensions).  Even using 20 quadrature points, in some cases the likelihoods do not increase monotonically between iterations.  This happens in mirt too; it gives the following warning (as mirt does check if likelihoods monotonically increase) :
Log-likelihood was decreasing near the ML solution. EM method may be unstable

In mirt, theta grid is used rather than Gaussian Quadratures.
I was amazing the speed of mirt. It turns out that the Estep function is written in C.

On Mon, Apr 30, 2018 at 5:00 PM, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Sun, Apr 29, 2018 at 11:08 PM uwbin <uwbi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > I am asking a programming question here. For confirmatory MIRT (e.g., multidimensional GPCM) and EM method, the population distribution parameters (e.g., the mean vector and sigma matrix of a multivariate normal distribution of population thetas)  need to be estimated.  In mirt, in the M (maximization) step  are all the first and second derivatives of the estimated parameter provided to the Newton-Raphson (NR) procedure? If so, could someone provide a reference for the derivatives of those population distribution parameters? Intuitively, you may update those parameters based on the posterior theta distribution in each iteration (e.g., the theta mean in an iteration  is just the mean of the posterior theta estimates of the previous iteration). However, I tried it and it did not work.
> > In general, does mirt provide the first and second derivatives of estimated parameter to a maximization routine or just use a existing maximization routine without providing derivative estimates?
>
> It depends on the algorithm used, and whether the latent trait components are freely estimated or not. The way you describe it works fine in the EM algorithm, but that's not what mirt does because the derivative information in the M-step is actually quite important from computing the ACOV matrix via the Oakes Identity approximation method. So in this case, the gradient and Hessian are computed from the MV normal distribution when this prior is assumed.
>
> Phil

messages.subject: Re: Confidence intervals for fscores
messages.subject_clean: Confidence intervals for fscores
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim,

If you apply the usual large sample symmetric interval then sure, you could obtain CIs. The reason that this isn't done by default is that many factor score computations include some Bayesian prior information (often borrowed from the model itself), so you don't really get CIs but rather the Bayesian analogue symmetric "credible regions", in which case the usual large-sample quantiles are not really kosher anymore. See below on how to compute CIs for ML estimates, in which this strategy is more in-line with theory.

#---------------------------
library(mirt)
mod <- mirt(Science, 1)
fs <- fscores(mod, full.scores.SE <http://full.scores.SE>=TRUE, method = 'ML')
head(fs)

# 95% large-sample symmetric CIs: x +- q * SE
CIs <- t(apply(fs, 1, function(x) x['F1'] + qnorm(c(.025, .975)) * x['SE_F1']))
head(CIs)
#---------------------------

Phil

> However, what does that exactly mean? Is “a1” referring to the discrimination of the items? Then what exactly does “d1” mean? That is not the difficulty of the item is it?

It depends entirely on the item types that you fitted. If you fit, for example, a 3PL model then your coefs would be a1, d, g, and u (fixed at 1); for a graded response model, you'd have a1, d1, d2, ..., dk-1. See coef(mod) to understand what you've fitted.

>                  to which.par”
>

d1 is not a valid parameter for your IRT model selected. You probably want something else.

>
> I am also struggling to understand the section where you are controlling for the latent variable. Do I need to use both “free_means” and “free_var” to control for laten variable? What does it really mean when I am controling for latent variable? Is that not the whole point of the DIF analysis, to check whether or not people with the same ability have the same probability of getting the item correct?

Freeing the latent mean/variance equates the groups so that the item parameters are on the same metric. Otherwise, observed differences in item response behaviour could be attributed to general group information differences rather than item bias (one would expect, for example, a 10th grad math class to have higher probabilities of answer questions correctly than a 9th grade class....but this doesn't mean the items are biased).

Phil

Yuxin

> Hello!

>
> Is possible to use mirt to calculate Conditional SEM?

Yes, just pass full.scores.SE <http://full.scores.SE> = TRUE to the fscores() function to obtain all the associated SEs for each vector. Then back convert these scores into the raw form via the expected.test() function.

>
> I also found fscores output produce the estimated ability to be in the range of -1 to 1. How to increase the range to -3 to 3? The Pearson bivariate correlation between students' estimated ability and their test results is 0.98. I found that is too high and is a bit counter intuitive.

Does it really matter? The metric for the ability terms is arbitrary and typically fixed with a mean of 0 variance 1.

And yes, such a high correlation with the total score makes a lot of sense. In the limiting case, where you have an infinite number of items, the total scores will converge to the exact ability parameters (this is true in both classical and modern test theory).

I know from previous work with unidimensional CAT in combination with EAP estimation, that by taking the posterior distribution of the last (interim) theta estimation as the prior for the next estimation cycle, only the answer to the last item has to be integrated (instead of the full response vector).

That's a clever idea, as it essentially trades RAM storage for repeated computations. Though I find that estimating theta is not the bottle neck in CATs, evaluating the remaining item pool criteria is.

>
> Is a similar 'trick' possible with multidimensional MAP estimation?
>
> From studying the mirtCAT documentation, I am guessing something like this might be possible, somewhere in the 'update' types of functions perhaps?

Unfortunately, no. With iterative algorithms the objective function must be evaluated multiple times throughout the search, and it's not clear what the theta will be after each iteration. That's nice, because it's essentially dimension free (doesn't require numerical integration), but bad because there's no real way to help it converge from previous information...other than providing starting values closer to the solution (which mirtCAT does by default based on the previous estimates).

messages.subject: Re: Effect Size for DIF and DTF
messages.subject_clean: Effect Size for DIF and DTF
messages.body_plain:
The paper I would start with is Meade's very nice article.

Meade, A. W. (2010). A taxonomy of effect size measures for the differential functioning of items and scales. Journal of Applied Psychology, 95, 728-743.

The DTF() statistics are in the family of the 'area' based measures, and so may not be completely the best summaries of DIF in that they don't contain information about the underlying density functions for the latent trait parameters. Some of the measures that Meade discusses do however try to include underlying density information either by approximating the terms first using so-called two-step methods or by assuming the density shape a priori (like in Stark and Wainer's measures). HTH.

Phil
